We need propose a retrosynthesis route with 1 reaction (i.e., one step) to target molecule: SMILES given with atom mapping: [CH2:1]=[C:2]([c:3]1[cH:4][cH:5][cH:6][cH:7][cH:8]1)[C@@H:9]1[CH2:10][CH2:11][CH2:12][C@@:13]1([OH:14])[C:15]([F:16])([F:17])[F:18]

Simplify: It's an alkene attached to phenyl (styrene) and attached to a cyclopentanol with CF3 group. So target is a product of carbonyl-ene reaction: starting from a ketone (maybe cyclopentanone with CF3) and an alkene (styrene). The carbonyl-ene would give allylic alcohol and form a new C-C bond, generating a five-membered ring? Actually carbonyl-ene between a carbonyl (ketone) and an alkene internal leads to a new C-C bond and an alcohol at the carbonyl carbon, forming a new C-C bond and a new stereocenter. The product would be a hydroxyalkyl attached to the alkene.

Thus retrosynthesis: disconnect the C-C bond formed between the alkene carbon (C2) and the carbonyl carbon (C9?). The product has a C-OH at C9 (the carbon originally carbonyl). So the precursor could be a ketone: cyclopentanone with CF3 at carbonyl carbon? Actually the product has a CF3 attached to C15 which is attached to C13 (the carbon bearing OH). In product, C13 is the carbon bearing OH and attached to CF3 group via C15? Wait: The SMILES: ...[C@@:13]1([OH:14])[C:15]([F:16])([F:17])[F:18]. So C13 is part of cyclopentane ring, bearing OH and attached to C15 which is CF3 carbon (C attached to three Fs). So the carbonyl precursor likely is a cyclopentanone where the carbonyl carbon is attached to CF3 (i.e., a trifluoromethyl ketone). That is, a cyclopentanone with CF3 at the carbonyl carbon (i.e., 2,2,2-trifluoro-1-cyclopentanone). The ene reaction with styrene would give the product where the carbonyl oxygen becomes OH, and the alkene attaches to the alpha carbon of the carbonyl (C9). So the precursor is: CF3-CO- (cyclopentane) (i.e., 2,2,2-trifluoro-1-cyclopentanone) plus styrene (C= C(c1ccccc1)H). The ene reaction forms a new bond between the alkene carbon (terminal CH2) and the carbonyl carbon? Actually ene reaction: alkene (ene) with allylic hydrogen reacts with carbonyl (enophile). The product: new C-C bond between the alkene's terminal carbon and the carbonyl carbon, and the carbonyl oxygen becomes OH, and the allylic hydrogen transfers to the carbonyl oxygen? Wait typical carbonyl-ene: R-CH=CH-CH2- + R'C=O -> R-CH-CH(R')-CH2-OH (allylic shift). So the new bond is between the alkene's terminal carbon (CH2) and the carbonyl carbon. The allylic hydrogen moves to the carbonyl oxygen, forming OH. So our product: the alkene is styrene: CH2=CH-Ph. The allylic hydrogen is on the carbon adjacent to the double bond (the CH2). After reaction, the CH2 becomes attached to carbonyl carbon, forming a new C-C bond, and the carbonyl oxygen becomes OH. So the product would have a CH2- attached to carbonyl carbon (now bearing OH). In our product, the double bond is now gone (C=C becomes C-C). Indeed product has a C-C bond between the former alkene carbon (C2) and the carbonyl carbon (C9). The product also has a new OH at carbonyl carbon (C14). So the precursor is: cyclopentanone with CF3 (trifluoromethyl ketone) and styrene.

Thus retrosynthesis: one reaction: carbonyl-ene between 2,2,2-trifluoro-1-cyclopentanone and styrene.
